items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: There used to be — well there was Shirley Scott who was this very good organ player who established herself.

ctx.x: I was curious if you think there’s a reason that women were sort of on the outside in jazz for so many years.

Well it would be several things. I mean one may be the question of attitude, you know, male superiority or whatever. The other may have been to some extent a practical matter. You know during the big band era the only women who were really involved were the singers and the singer usually had to hook up with one of the guys in the band, either marry them or be the girlfriend of, in order to be protected from the usual male stuff. So that was another reason maybe why even if there was, or had been, a really…

there was a shortage of women who were prepared to really cope with all these obstacles. Woody Herman had a very good trumpet player named Billie Rogers who was in the band during World War II, and that was one moment where there was a little bit of that. You would suddenly find some female musicians in the sections of a big band. I think Lionel Hampton had a girl tenor player. There were isolated instances of that, and that’s because so many guys were getting drafted and there was a shortage of competent…
